teaser: Tiny holes. A little water. Where does a squeeze send it?
title: A Kitchen Sponge
question: Where does the water go, and how much can one sponge hold?
idea: A sponge has connected spaces that draw in water. A squeeze makes those spaces smaller and pushes water out.

curiosity.intro: A little spill disappears into a sponge. Where did the water go?
curiosity.carryForward: Follow the water into the holes, into the cup, and into a new question.

questions.question: What is inside all those holes?
questions.notice: The magnifier makes the sponge’s open spaces easier to notice.
questions.say: A kitchen sponge has pores: tiny holes leading into connected spaces. Water can travel through these spaces, like little tunnels. Most kitchen sponges are made by people from cellulose, a plant fibre, or foam. Many sea sponges are simple animals; this kitchen sponge is a made object.
questions.try: Find two holes, then imagine a path between spaces inside.

questions.question: How does water move into the sponge?
questions.notice: The sponge’s wet edge grows darker as it touches water.
questions.say: Water clings to the sponge’s walls and creeps along narrow gaps. We call this spreading wicking. To absorb means to take water in. Some water is held inside the connected spaces, so you cannot see all of it from outside.
questions.try: With Big leading, use a new, clean sponge, a tray, two clear cups, and a measuring spoon. Dip, lift, and squeeze over the empty cup. Wipe up drips so the floor stays dry.

questions.question: Why does a squeeze bring the water back?
questions.notice: Drops fall from the squeezed sponge into the cup.
questions.say: Squeezing presses the sponge’s walls closer together. There is less room inside, so water is pushed out. Let go, and the springy material opens back up. It can soak up water again.
questions.try: Compare the sponge’s shape during a squeeze and after you let go.

questions.question: Would a damp sponge soak up a spill faster?
questions.notice: Two same-size pieces meet equal little spills for the same time.
questions.say: A damp sponge often starts soaking faster than a bone-dry one. Damp means a little wet, not full of water. Compare fairly: use the same kind and size of sponge, equal amounts of water, and the same time. Look at how much of each spill is left.
questions.try: Predict which spill will shrink faster, then compare what is left.

reading.title: Where did the water go?
reading.coverText: A sponge takes in a little spill. A squeeze brings the water back. Follow its path.
reading.foldableNote: Dip, squeeze, notice, and pause whenever you like.
reading.parentNote: Age 8 / Grade 3 reading. Welcome spoken answers and dictation. Connect sponge, pores, soak, squeeze, spring back, and absorb to the tray experiment.

outline.arc: Little follows water through a sponge’s connected spaces, sees a squeeze bring it back, compares dry and damp pieces fairly, watches the sponge reopen, and keeps a question about how much it can hold.

beatIntents.intent: Establish the warm kitchen table, a fresh golden cellulose sponge, brass magnifier, tray, two clear cups, Big and Little, and a linen notebook; focus on visible pores and the opening question.
Big lowers the same sponge into a shallow dish on the tray; Little notices the wet edge creeping upward. Keep the sponge in contact with the water, with no floating drops.
Big compresses the same sponge above an empty clear cup inside the tray. Water travels down into the cup; Little watches the connection between smaller spaces and released water.

Compare two same-size pieces of the same sponge with equal small puddles and equal time, one initially dry and one damp. A split tray and small timer support the comparison; no numerical results are painted.
After the squeeze, show the released sponge fully open on the tray next to the partly filled cup. The pair notice its restored shape; depict one actual sponge, no motion duplicates.
Return to the notebook with a wordless drawing of a sponge and a clear cup; Big sits beside Little. Keep the opening water question alive with the same tray and magnifier.

beats.title: A question full of holes
beats.passage: Little Wonderer peered through a magnifier at a kitchen sponge. A sponge is a soft material that can take in water. “It is full of holes!” Little said. “Those holes are pores,” said Big. Inside, many spaces connect like little tunnels. Little wondered where a spill would go.
beats.prompt: How could connected holes help water move?

beats.title: Water finds a way
beats.passage: Big dipped the sponge into a shallow dish. Its lower edge grew darker. Water clung to the sponge’s walls and crept into narrow gaps. This slow spreading is called wicking. To soak up, or absorb, means to take water in. The water was entering the spaces inside.
beats.prompt: What does the darker wet edge help Little notice?

beats.title: A squeeze into the cup
beats.passage: Big lifted the sponge over an empty cup. “Where is the water now?” asked Little. Big gave a gentle squeeze: a press from both sides. The spaces became smaller, pushing water out. Drops fell into the cup. The water had not vanished. Little could see it again.
beats.prompt: What evidence shows that the water did not vanish?

beats.title: Two little spills
beats.passage: Next they compared two same-size pieces. One was bone-dry; the other was damp, with a little water already inside. Each met the same small spill for the same time. The damp piece soaked up its spill faster. That often happens, but different sponges can behave differently. A fair test helps us find out.
beats.prompt: Why keep the piece size, water, and time the same?

beats.title: Open again
beats.passage: Big let go after another squeeze. The sponge began to spring back, returning to its open shape. Its spaces opened too, ready to take in water again. “Smaller, then open,” Little said. The sponge changed shape, but the water stayed water. Little sketched the cup beside it.
beats.prompt: How does springing back help the sponge soak again?

beats.title: A question to keep
beats.passage: “Is our sponge an animal?” Little asked. “Sea sponges are simple animals,” said Big. “People make most kitchen sponges from cellulose, a plant fibre, or foam.” Little drew holes in the notebook. “How much could ours hold?”
beats.prompt: How is this kitchen sponge different from a sea sponge?

math.title: Compare a little water
math.intro: For a comparison, put >, <, or = in the circle. For rounding, write the nearest ten.

tasks.prompt: Little squeezes 32 millilitres of water into one cup and 47 into another. Which symbol compares the amounts?
tasks.hint: Compare the tens first. Three tens is less than four tens.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big measures 63 millilitres of water squeezed from a sponge. What is that amount rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Find the nearby tens, 60 and 70. The ones digit is less than 5.
tasks.worked: 63 rounds to 60. It is 3 away from 60 and 7 away from 70.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: A sponge soaks up 58 millilitres and a cloth soaks up 51 millilitres in a test. Which symbol compares the amounts?
tasks.hint: The tens match. Compare 8 ones with 1 one.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Little counts 25 visible holes in a close-up sponge sketch. What is that count rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: 25 is halfway between 20 and 30. When the ones digit is 5, round up.
tasks.worked: 25 rounds to 30. Halfway counts round up to the next ten.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Little counts 76 drops in one cup and 89 in another after a squeeze. Which symbol compares the counts?
tasks.hint: Compare 7 tens with 8 tens before looking at the ones.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: The measuring cup holds 97 millilitres from several sponge squeezes. What is that amount rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: The nearby tens are 90 and 100. A ones digit of 7 rounds up.
tasks.worked: 97 rounds to 100. It is 3 away from 100 and 7 away from 90.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one answer and explain how the tens and ones helped you.
math.parentNote: Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Three two-digit comparisons and three nearest-ten rounding tasks. Rounding is a requested extension. A ones digit of 5 rounds up. The comparison answer key gives the greater number and the completed comparison. These story quantities are practice data, not measurements of the paintings or sponge capacity.
math.actionLabel: Compare or round to the nearest ten

math.answerKeyIntro: Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Compare tens and ones. For rounding, locate the two nearby tens; a halfway value rounds up. Welcome spoken reasoning or a number line.

parentGuidance: Age 8, Grade 3 reading, and Grade 2 math. Lead the optional water test with a new, clean sponge, not the used dish sponge. Use a tray, two clear cups, a measuring cup or spoon, and water. Dip, lift, squeeze over a cup, and compare amounts. Wipe up drips so floors stay dry. Water enters connected pores through wetting and capillary action; cellulose fibres also take up water. Damp cellulose often wets faster than bone-dry cellulose, but materials vary. Compare same-size pieces of the same material, equal water, and equal time. For uptake speed, compare water left in the dishes. Water squeezed from a damp sponge includes water already present, so cup volume alone is not a fair measure of newly absorbed water. The diorama shows qualitative levels during one short dip, not millilitres, capacity, or guaranteed results. It keeps a small amount of water in the sponge after squeezing. Most kitchen sponges are manufactured from cellulose or foam; sea sponges are animals.

authoring.learningRule: Leo is age 8, Grade 3 for reading; math is Grade 2. New Curiosity packs declare mathTemplate and require exactly six tasks for that template. Every number (operands, terms, intermediates, answers) is an integer from 0 to 100. Each task asks one clear question tied to the day's story and includes an equation matching the validated numbers, a hint, numeric answer, and short worked explanation containing the answer (mixed-review retains its shipped calculation rule). Replace scaffold notebook objects with the day's story objects. Explain precise vocabulary in context; welcome speech and dictation. Template compare-and-round: Six tasks including both two-digit comparisons and nearest-ten rounding (a requested extension). Compare uses two operands, symbol >|<|=, and equation a ○ b: put the symbol in the circle and give the greater number as the numeric answer (the shared number if equal); the worked step shows the completed comparison (e.g. 47 < 74). Round-ten uses one two-digit operand and equation n → nearest ten: ___; 5 rounds up, at most 100.

questions.prompt: Where does water go when a kitchen sponge absorbs it?
questions.answer: Water enters connected spaces inside the sponge. It clings to the walls and creeps into narrow gaps.

choices: The spaces get smaller and push water out
questions.answer: Squeezing makes the spaces smaller and pushes water out. Releasing the sponge lets it spring back open.

questions.prompt: How can Little compare soaking speed fairly?
choices: Use same-size pieces, equal water, and the same time
Give one piece more water and more time
Use two different sizes and guess
questions.answer: Use same-size pieces of the same kind of sponge, equal amounts of water, and the same time. Compare the water left in the spills.
